analysis.one_liner: Directs federal safety agencies to study workplace violence and publish voluntary prevention guidance for employers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2024 and referred to committee, but received no vote or further action before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health study how to reduce violence against workers, then require the Labor Department's workplace safety agency to publish voluntary guidance — tailored to settings like stores, hospitals, restaurants, and schools — on measures such as barriers, alarms, security staffing, and de-escalation training. Because the guidance is nonmandatory, employers would not be required to follow it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in jobs where they face customers, patients, or the public face-to-face — retail clerks, grocery and pharmacy workers, hospital and nursing staff, restaurant and bar employees, transit and social-service workers, and school staff. They would gain a federal playbook of concrete prevention measures (barriers, alarms, weapon detectors, staffing levels, training) and official recognition of workplace violence as a hazard worth addressing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retail, grocery, healthcare, and restaurant workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires NIOSH to study reducing the threat of violence in the workplace and report recommendations to the Labor Department and Congress within 15 months of enactment.

Directs OSHA to issue nonmandatory guidance, within four years of enactment, on engineering controls (such as electronic access controls, weapon detectors, shatter-resistant glass, deep service counters, alarms, and video monitoring) and work practice controls (such as adequate staffing, security personnel, and de-escalation and response training).

Requires the guidance to be tailored to different workplace types, including grocery stores, retail stores, movie theatres, hospitals, restaurants and bars, and schools, recognizing that violence risks differ by setting.
Defines workplace violence broadly to include threats and incidents that cause fear, trauma, or stress even when no physical injury occurs, excluding lawful self-defense.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in the covered industries would face the cost of any prevention measures they choose to adopt — equipment, staffing, security, and training — though the guidance being nonmandatory means nothing would be required. Federal agencies would absorb modest costs for the study and guidance development.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, voluntarily; only guidance, no mandates

drawbacks.text: The guidance is nonmandatory, so no employer would be legally required to implement any of the recommended protections; workers in dangerous settings would get a reference document, not enforceable safety rules.
The timeline is slow — a report within 15 months and guidance not required until four years after enactment — meaning no practical effect until well into a future Congress.

Prevention measures such as adequate staffing and dedicated security personnel impose real ongoing costs on labor-intensive businesses like hospitals and grocery stores, and voluntary guidance could nonetheless become a benchmark in lawsuits or union negotiations, which is why some employers oppose any movement toward workplace violence standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits to workers are real but modest: voluntary guidance can raise awareness and shape practice, but it cannot compel any employer to act, and the four-year timeline delays even that. The cost to employers is low precisely because nothing is mandatory. An honest assessment is that this is a small, cautious first step — the strongest version of the idea would be enforceable standards, and this bill deliberately stops short of that.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse (D-CO) introduced the Safe Workplaces Act on June 7, 2024, with three Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — is recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in retail, healthcare, and hospitality are better off because no guidance — even voluntary — was developed, and no precedent toward enforceable workplace violence protections was set. Workers in violence-prone jobs gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided even voluntary safety guidance

sides.party_line_note: All four initial sponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican supported or opposed the bill on the record; the bill never advanced far enough for a partisan vote to reveal the split.

industries.note: The bill targets violence against front-line retail and grocery workers, a sector with frequent customer assaults, and its recommendations (barriers, alarms, staffing, security) would impose costs if adopted. Because the guidance is nonmandatory, the cost is voluntary and modest.

Healthcare settings are explicitly named, and violence against nurses and aides is a recognized hazard; staffing and security recommendations would carry real ongoing costs. The nonmandatory design keeps the burden minimal.

Named in the bill as a workplace type to receive tailored guidance; alcohol-service settings face elevated violence risk, and any adopted measures (staffing, training, physical controls) would be an expense. Nothing would be required.
